statements.reason: Matches the providers' hope and leadership's worry about a breach and accuracy.

statements.statement: Staff, volunteers, contractors and board members, at both locations.

statements.statement: EHR AI scribe: Three-provider pilot, business associate agreement signed. May hold patient information in those visits.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Beth described the signed BAA and the three-provider pilot as the only approved AI.

statements.statement: Nadia (privacy and security officer) approves any new tool or AI feature that could touch patient information, after a business associate agreement.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Beth said Nadia approves any tool that could touch PHI and a BAA comes first.

statements.statement: Use your work email. Turn off any vendor setting that trains on what you type.
statements.label: default
statements.reason: The call was silent on accounts; this is the template default.

statements.section: What you can use AI for
statements.statement: Everyone, now: Any AI tool, through your work email, for work with no information about a real person.
statements.label: default
statements.reason: The call settled nothing for everyone and did not say no, so the template default applies.

statements.section: What you can use AI for
statements.statement: Appointment reminder and sliding fee letter templates, with no patient details.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Jordan said staff use ChatGPT for these letters, hopefully without names, which fits the Everyone, now rule.

statements.section: What you can use AI for
statements.statement: Patient education handouts, with no patient details.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Dr. Okafor said some use ChatGPT for handouts, and this works under Everyone, now.

statements.section: What you can use AI for
statements.statement: Clinicians: general clinical lookups with no patient information.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Dr. Okafor described OpenEvidence and UpToDate AI lookups with no patient information, which Everyone, now allows.

statements.section: What you can use AI for
statements.statement: Pilot providers: scribe-drafted visit notes.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: The scribe is approved for the three-provider pilot and the draft is reviewed before signing.

statements.statement: Patient information in any tool beyond the scribe pilot — Nadia, privacy and security officer
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Nadia approves any tool that could touch PHI, with a BAA first.

statements.statement: Any other clinical use — Dr. Okafor, medical director
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Beth said clinical uses need Dr. Okafor.

statements.statement: Billing or coding help — Your manager
statements.label: default
statements.reason: The call named billing as risky but no approver, so the manager default applies.

statements.statement: Information that never goes into an AI tool, unless approved above: diagnoses, medications, behavioral health notes, HIV status and reproductive health (HIPAA).
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Beth listed these as the protected health information the clinic holds.

statements.statement: Substance use treatment records, with extra federal protection. Immigration status, sliding fee income documents, insurance numbers, staff files, the donor list, and all passwords.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: All were named on the call; passwords are always protected.

statements.statement: No tool that could touch patient information without a business associate agreement.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Beth said a BAA is required first, no exceptions.

statements.statement: AI never makes a clinical decision or signs a note.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Dr. Okafor said a clinician decides and signs.

statements.section: Check everything before it goes out
statements.statement: A clinician reviews every word of AI notes and handouts before signing or sending. Check medications, names, numbers, tone.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Dr. Okafor said the provider reviews every word; Jordan said a clinician should review handouts.

statements.section: Check everything before it goes out
statements.statement: A person checks billing and coding suggestions. Whoever sends it is responsible.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Beth raised billing and coding errors as a Medicaid compliance risk.

statements.statement: A person, not AI, decides sliding fee eligibility and who gets services. AI may help a clinician look things up.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Beth said a person decides eligibility; Dr. Okafor said AI may help a clinician look things up.

statements.statement: Tell patients when the scribe is listening, and let them say no.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Dr. Okafor described the verbal consent script used in the pilot.

statements.statement: If we add a patient chatbot, it must say it is not a person.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Jordan said patients should know a chatbot is not a person.

statements.statement: Tell Nadia right away. She runs the HIPAA breach clock.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Dr. Okafor said problems go to Nadia, who runs the breach process.

statements.statement: Reporting a mistake is expected, never punished.
statements.label: default
statements.reason: Template default; the call was silent on this.

statements.statement: The compliance committee reviews this policy; the board approves it.
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Beth said the board approves it and the compliance committee reviews it first.

statements.statement: After the pilot, do we roll the scribe out to all providers, and should behavioral health use it?
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Beth left both decisions open and the policy does not settle them elsewhere.

statements.statement: Which tools staff use now, like ChatGPT, OpenEvidence and UpToDate AI, do we approve or pay for?
statements.label: contradicts
statements.reason: Everyone, now allows any AI tool and the allowed uses depend on these tools, so the policy partly settles this; reword the question to ask about paying or approving them for patient information.

statements.statement: Who checks AI or Google Translate versions of Spanish patient materials?
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Jordan raised this risk and the call settled no process.

statements.statement: What do we tell funders, like HRSA, who ask about AI?
statements.label: supported
statements.reason: Beth said funders haven't asked yet but will; nothing is settled.

missed: Translation of patient materials, including Google Translate for Spanish, is not covered in any rule; staff get no guidance until the open question is answered.
No rule says whether ChatGPT letters may include patient names; Jordan hoped staff leave names out but this is not stated for staff.
The policy does not say how staff learn it, even though staff are unsure what is allowed and some use AI secretly.
The behavioral health team's exclusion from the scribe pilot is not stated; staff cannot tell whether those providers may use it now.
Staff worry about being replaced by a phone bot; the policy does not address how AI relates to staff jobs.
